subject.title: Ode on Solitude
subject.author: Alexander Pope
subject.text:
Happy the man, whose wish and care
   A few paternal acres bound,
Content to breathe his native air,
                            In his own ground.

Whose herds with milk, whose fields with bread,
   Whose flocks supply him with attire,
Whose trees in summer yield him shade,
                            In winter fire.

Blest, who can unconcernedly find
   Hours, days, and years slide soft away,
In health of body, peace of mind,
                            Quiet by day,

Sound sleep by night; study and ease,
   Together mixed; sweet recreation;
And innocence, which most does please,
                            With meditation.

Thus let me live, unseen, unknown;
   Thus unlamented let me die;
Steal from the world, and not a stone
                            Tell where I lie.

title: Unseen, Unknown, and Extensively Documented
standfirst: Pope's ode asks to die without so much as a stone marking the spot. His own biographer caught him moving the dates on his early poems to look more precocious, and bibliographers still can't agree on the year this one first reached print.

sections.heading: Not a Stone to Tell Where He Lay
A Family Displaced, a Boy Praising the Ground
sections.body: Pope said he wrote this at twelve, in 1700 — the same year his father, a Catholic linen-draper, moved the household out of London for good. A statute barred Catholics from living within ten miles of London or Westminster, and the family resettled on [a small estate at Binfield](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Alexander_Pope), in Windsor Forest. Formal schooling was closed to him too: Catholics could not attend university, and after two Catholic schools near Winchester and at Hyde Park Corner, he was left to teach himself, later recalling that "in a few years I had dipped into a great number of the English, French, Italian, Latin, and Greek poets." He had also lived from early childhood with Pott's disease, a tubercular infection of the spine that would stop his growth at four foot six. None of that reads like a cheerful volunteer for solitude. More like a boy for whom small acres and a shut door were simply what was left to him.

sections.heading: Twelve, According to the Author
sections.body: Every retelling of this poem repeats that Pope wrote it at twelve; almost none pause on where that date comes from. It comes from Pope. He made the same claim for a lost paraphrase of Thomas à Kempis written, he said, at the same age, and his early biographer [Leslie Stephen concluded](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Alexander_Pope_%28Stephen%29/Chapter_2) flatly that "Pope was eager for the praise of remarkable precocity, and was weak and insincere enough to alter the dates of some of his writings in order to strengthen his claim." Stephen still thought the underlying talent was real — "even when we accept the corrected accounts of recent enquirers," he wrote, the command of the form is genuinely early. But the number twelve is Pope's own figure, filed by a man with a documented habit of moving his dates around to look more precocious than he was.

sections.heading: One Bibliography Says 1726
sections.body: The dating trouble doesn't stop at composition. Several poetry sites now describe the poem as published the same year it was written, in 1700, right after the move to Binfield. The print record disagrees by a generous margin: according to [Reginald Griffith's standard bibliography of Pope](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Solitude_%28Pope%29), the poem's first appearance in print was in 1726, in the fifth edition of a multi-author miscellany called *Miscellaneous Poems, Translation and Imitations by Several Hands* — twenty-six years after the boy who supposedly wrote it put down his pen, and nine years after Pope's first collected *Works*. Nobody retelling this story, Pope included, seems to have been especially interested in getting the paperwork straight.

sections.heading: Beatus Ille, Anglicised
sections.body: The opening is not really Pope's own idea. Horace's second epode begins *Beatus ille qui procul negotiis* — happy the man who, far from business affairs — and [Pope's first line](https://americanliterature.com/author/alexander-pope/poem/ode-on-solitude) all but translates it: "Happy the man, whose wish and care / A few paternal acres bound." What he adds is the shape. Each of the five stanzas runs three lines of iambic tetrameter cut short by a fourth line of dimeter, so every stanza physically contracts before it ends, a small formal echo of the retreat it describes. The rhymes are almost too neat for a real farm — bound/ground, attire/fire — except once: bread is left to rhyme against shade, the one stanza where even the sound refuses to close all the way.

sections.heading: Wordsworth Copied It Out, Precocity Note and All
sections.body: By 1819 the twelve-year-old story had already hardened into fact. That Christmas, William Wordsworth compiled a private manuscript anthology as a gift for a friend, Lady Mary Lowther, copying favourite poems out in his own hand. He [included this one](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Poems_and_Extracts/Ode_on_Solitude), attributed in his own note to "Pope, in his 12th year," alongside verse by Anne Finch and others. The album stayed a private family object for the Lowthers for nearly a century before it was finally printed in facsimile in 1905. A schoolroom claim about a twelve-year-old's precocity had, by then, survived one of England's most exacting poets copying it into a keepsake without a flicker of doubt.
